lesson.title: The Missed Signal: Understanding Type II Error
lesson.summary: A Type II error happens when you fail to reject a null hypothesis that is actually false, a missed real effect, making it the mirror image of a Type I error.
lesson.body:
A Type II error occurs when a test fails to reject H0 even though H0 is actually false, meaning Ha is actually true. It is a false negative, or a missed detection: there really was a difference or effect out in the world, but the sample evidence was not strong enough to catch it, so p ended up greater than or equal to alpha. The probability of a Type II error is conventionally labeled beta. The details of exactly what makes beta larger or smaller belong to the study of a test's power, but the core idea belongs here: beta measures how often a real effect slips past a test completely undetected.

Continuing the courtroom analogy, where H0 stands for "the defendant is innocent," a Type II error is acquitting a truly guilty defendant: the evidence presented at trial simply was not convincing enough to meet the "beyond a reasonable doubt" bar, even though the person genuinely committed the crime.

Here is a concrete scenario grounded in the cereal box example, without needing to compute beta itself. Suppose the filling machine has actually drifted so that boxes now average 15.85 ounces, not 16. That is a real, genuine underfill, H0: mu = 16 is false. If the inspector's sample of 36 boxes happens to come back with a sample mean close to 16, say 15.98 ounces, a result well within ordinary sampling variation and not far enough from 16 to produce a small p-value, the test would fail to reject H0: mu = 16, even though the machine really is off. That is a Type II error: a genuine problem existed in the population, and this particular sample simply was not extreme enough to reveal it.

Because a Type II error's likelihood depends on how far the true parameter actually sits from the null value, how much sampling variability is present, and what alpha was chosen, it is tightly linked to decisions made when a test is designed. That link sets up the next two chapters, choosing alpha and error tradeoffs, where Type I and Type II error are weighed against each other directly.
